reconcile.connective: Gill reads the postures as sequential: sitting when Mary Magdalene alone first looked in, then risen and standing by the time the rest of the women arrived, which is what Luke records.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible catalogs Mark and John's 'sitting' against Luke's 'stood' as a flat, unreconciled contradiction in posture.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/sitting.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: …John makes mention of two, as here, seen by Mary Magdalene, though in a different posture; they were sitting, the one at the head, the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain; but when the rest of the women came, they were risen up, and stood close by them, on a sudden, at an unawares …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles John's 'sitting' with Luke's 'stood' by proposing a sequence: the angels were seated when Mary Magdalene looked in alone, then rose to their feet once the rest of the women reached the tomb.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Under 'Christ's resurrection, — certain narratives. A different account of it.' (Historical Discrepancies, pp. 327-331), Haley reproduces Robinson's and Ebrard's harmonized sequence of the resurrection-morning events, which folds in the detail that Mary Magdalene, looking into the sepulchre, 'saw two angels sitting' before the rest of the women's party arrived — treating the whole composite narrative rather than isolating the sitting/standing wording under its own heading.
